summary:
Legal gender recognition in Mexico is granted through state-level administrative procedures rather than a single national statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 32 of the country's states have legislated such a procedure, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Coahuila de Zaragoza belongs to the states that have acted.

Coahuila de Zaragoza's 2018 Law on the Civil Registry, at articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for the recognition of self-identified gender identity. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records the provision and links the official gazette text of the reform. A trans visitor to Coahuila can therefore expect a legal route to a matching identity document that does not depend on litigation.

The measure was enacted by the state congress in 2018 out of proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira. The dictamen was approved unanimously; it reformed article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and created the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI defines gender identity as a person's personal and internal conviction.

Take-up is documented. Ricardo Malacara, director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, stated on 31 March 2023 that around 1,500 people had completed the gender-identity change procedure before the Civil Registry from early 2019 to March 2023, in both directions between male and female. The procedure is thus used and processed in practice, not dormant on the statute book.

Recognition of documents does not settle physical safety. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 in the twelve months to September 2023, a national figure second only to Brazil's 100. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Coahuila de Zaragoza and no state law targets trans presence.
tangentialFactors:
States without a recognition procedure illustrate what Coahuila de Zaragoza's law avoids. Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that Tabasco has no administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, that the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, that Tabasco's criminal code carries no hate-motivation provisions, and that healthcare staff out patients by calling them by their legal names. The same report found that delays and refusals elsewhere leave trans residents holding documents that contradict their lived identity, with knock-on discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

The national violence picture remains severe. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide on 18 July 2024 with sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case is unpunished; the report placed the statute in one of the region's deadliest settings for trans people and noted that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

Attacks intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the point directly: the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Coahuila's administrative recognition procedure sits inside that wider environment of under-enforcement.
localsOnly:
Roughly 1,500 residents completed the legal gender-identity change before Coahuila's Civil Registry between early 2019 and March 2023, according to Civil Registry director Ricardo Malacara, with registrations recorded in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Malacara further stated on 31 March 2023 that approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in the state, a figure that speaks to workplace participation rather than to visitor risk.

The recognition route runs administratively through the Civil Registry under articles 124 to 128 of the 2018 Law on the Civil Registry, so residents are not directed to a court petition for a name and gender change. Gender identity is defined in the statute itself at article 2, fraction XI, as the personal and internal conviction of the person.
outOfScopeNotes:
No incident of violence against a trans person in Coahuila de Zaragoza, and no enforcement failure by Coahuila authorities, appears in the source inventory; the absence of such reporting in these sources is unresolved rather than evidence that none occurs, given the national impunity figures cited above.

Whether Coahuila de Zaragoza's criminal code contains hate-motivation or aggravated-penalty provisions for crimes against LGBT people is not sourced here. The inventory documents the absence of such provisions in Tabasco only.

The procedural mechanics of Coahuila's recognition route are not sourced: fees, processing times, documentary requirements such as medical or psychological assessments, residency thresholds, and whether minors can access the procedure are unresolved.

Human Rights Watch warns that implementation of recognition procedures differs sharply between states, but the inventory supplies no Coahuila-specific assessment of how the procedure is administered in practice, including any refusals or delays. The 1,500 completed cases indicate volume, not quality.
